BoRP: Bootstrapped Regression Probing for
Scalable and Human-Aligned LLM Evaluation

Peng Sun ††thanks: Corresponding author.    Xiangyu Zhang    and Duan Wu Affiliation: Alibaba Group Email: sp80287@alibaba-inc.com
Abstract

Accurate evaluation of user satisfaction is critical for iterative development of conversational AI. However, for open-ended assistants, traditional A/B testing lacks reliable metrics: explicit feedback is sparse, while implicit metrics are ambiguous. To bridge this gap, we introduce BoRP (Bootstrapped Regression Probing), a scalable framework for high-fidelity satisfaction evaluation. Unlike generative approaches, BoRP leverages the geometric properties of LLM latent space. It employs a polarization-index-based bootstrapping mechanism to automate rubric generation and utilizes Partial Least Squares (PLS) to map hidden states to continuous scores. Experiments on industrial datasets show that BoRP (Qwen3-8B/14B) significantly outperforms generative baselines (even Qwen3-Max) in alignment with human judgments. Furthermore, BoRP reduces inference costs by orders of magnitude, enabling full-scale monitoring and highly sensitive A/B testing via CUPED.

1 Introduction

With the advent of LLMs, conversational agents have shifted towards unstructured, open-ended interactions, enabling users to fulfill diverse intents. This flexibility, however, complicates satisfaction quantification. Traditional heuristic metrics (e.g., Session Duration, Turn Counts) suffer from ambiguity Deriu et al. (2021): prolonged engagement can signal either immersion or confusion. Conversely, posterior metrics like Retention (R1/R7) act as lagging indicators, lacking the sensitivity required for rapid strategy iteration. This creates a critical "Metric Gap": the industry urgently needs a framework to capture immediate satisfaction with high fidelity.

The Dilemma of Existing Paradigms

Existing evaluation methodologies primarily fall into four categories, yet each hits a "hard wall" in industrial deployment.

Manual Evaluation, while serving as the gold standard, is blocked by the Wall of Scalability. The sparsity of human labels results in insufficient statistical power for A/B testing Kohavi et al. (2020). Consequently, detecting small but meaningful strategy improvements requires impractically long experiment durations.

Generative Evaluation (LLM-as-a-Judge) suffers from an irreconcilable Accuracy-Cost Trade-off. Using SOTA models (e.g., GPT-4) incurs prohibitive costs for full-scale monitoring. Conversely, smaller models (e.g., 7B-14B) often exhibit an "Alignment Tax"—a central tendency bias that suppresses extreme judgments. Furthermore, recent research Zhu et al. (2025) reveals the intrinsic instability of generative judgments, where stochastic decoding leads to inconsistent scores, necessitating expensive aggregation strategies to ensure reliability.

Fine-tuned Evaluators (Specialized Judges & BERT) attempt to bridge the gap by training on evaluation-specific datasets. Recent works like Prometheus Kim et al. (2024), JudgeLM Zhu et al. (2023), and JudgeLRM Yuan and others (2025) have shown promise by fine-tuning LLMs on massive feedback datasets (often >100​k>100k samples) . However, this paradigm faces two hurdles: (1) Data Scalability: Curating such large-scale, high-quality reasoning traces is prohibitively expensive for every new business domain. (2) Inference Cost: Being generative in nature, they still incur high decoding latency. On the other end, traditional discriminative fine-tuning (e.g., BERT) is fast but limited by a Cognitive Bottleneck, lacking the reasoning depth to evaluate complex multi-turn logic in open-ended chat.

Conventional Probing (typically linear classifiers or PCA), while efficient, often settles for Coarse Classification. Even recent works Maiya et al. (2025) focusing on preference extraction remain limited to pairwise ranking or binary judgments. Unsupervised probes are easily distracted by "Topic Residuals"—where the high variance of conversation topics overshadows subtle sentiment signals Burns et al. (2022), making them unsuitable for fine-grained ordinal regression in industrial settings.

Present Work

To bridge these gaps, we introduce BoRP (Bootstrapped Regression Probing), an end-to-end framework designed to break the "impossible triangle" of quality, cost, and coverage in industrial evaluation. We reframe evaluation not as generation, but as a high-fidelity regression task within the latent space.

Contributions

Our main contributions are four-fold:

  • •

    Methodological Innovation: We propose a Geometry-Aware Regression approach. By introducing Partial Least Squares (PLS)Wold (1966) and a Polarization-guided resampling strategy, we effectively identify satisfaction-related subspaces within high-dimensional noise, outperforming PCA and generative baselines in fine-grained scoring.

  • •

    Data Efficiency: We design a Probe-Guided Bootstrapping mechanism. By defining a Polarization Index to unsupervisedly mine extreme samples and employing ensemble distillation, we automate rubric generation, significantly reducing the reliance on expert knowledge.

  • •

    System Performance: We implement a high-throughput inference engine leveraging Suffix-Only Probing and KV-Cache Reuse. This achieves an industrial-scale throughput of approx. 1.4M sessions/day on a single GPU, reducing costs by two orders of magnitude compared to GPT-4.

  • •

    Industrial Impact: We validate BoRP in large-scale online A/B testing. Combined with CUPED, our framework demonstrates superior sensitivity, effectively guiding rapid product iteration.

2 Related Work

LLM-as-a-Judge & Specialized Models

Evaluating open-ended generation has shifted from n-gram metrics (BLEU) to model-based evaluation. Early works prompted proprietary models like GPT-4 Zheng et al. (2024); Chang et al. (2024). Recent efforts focus on fine-tuning specialized judge models, such as Prometheus Kim et al. (2024), JudgeLM Zhu et al. (2023), and JudgeLRM Yuan and others (2025), to improve alignment. While effective, these generative approaches suffer from high inference latency and inherent biases (e.g., position bias Wang et al. (2023a), verbosity bias Saito et al. (2023)). Furthermore, recent studies highlight the calibration issues and instability of generative scoring Verga et al. (2025); Zhu et al. (2025). BoRP addresses these by bypassing generation entirely.

Automated Rubric Generation

Defining high-quality rubrics is a bottleneck for evaluation. Recent works like OpenRubrics Zhang et al. (2025), Auto-Rubric Wang et al. (2025), and Rubrics-as-Rewards Lee et al. (2025) explore using LLMs to synthesize or refine evaluation criteria. While promising, these methods typically rely on prompting strategies (e.g., "Write a rubric for X"). In contrast, BoRP introduces a Geometry-Guided approach: we use the Polarization Index to mine real-world extreme samples from unlabeled data, ensuring that the generated rubrics are grounded in the actual distribution of the industrial traffic.

Latent Probing & Uncertainty

Probing classifiers have been used to interpret internal representations Alain and Bengio (2016), detecting truthfulness Burns et al. (2022) or hallucinations. However, most probes focus on binary classification. BoRP advances this by introducing PLS regression for fine-grained ordinal scoring (1-5 scale). Additionally, leveraging insights from uncertainty estimation surveys Huang et al. (2025); Chen et al. (2025), we explore layer-wise consistency as a computation-free proxy for model confidence, enabling reliable human-in-the-loop deployment.

Efficient Inference

Techniques like FlashAttention Dao et al. (2022) and RadixAttention (SGLang) Zheng et al. (2023) have revolutionized throughput. Our work explicitly leverages the KV-Cache separation property of these frameworks to implement our "Suffix-Only" architecture, maximizing the ROI of inference infrastructure.

3 Methodology

We propose BoRP, a geometry-aware framework for scalable LLM evaluation. As illustrated in Figure 1, the system architecture comprises a Bootstrapping Engine (Figure 1 Left) and a Probing Engine (Figure 1 Right). We detail the mathematical formulation of latent representations in Sec 3.1, followed by the bootstrapping mechanism (Sec 3.2), regression algorithm (Sec 3.3), and system optimization (Sec 3.4).

3.1 Preliminaries: Contrastive Representation

Following Burns et al. (2022), we extract representations from the model’s internal states. For a dialogue HH and query UU, we construct a positive prompt Pp​o​sP_{pos} and a negative prompt Pn​e​gP_{neg} (using generic templates initially). We extract the hidden states of the final token at the last layer:

𝐯d​i​f​f=ℳ⁡(H,U,Pp​o​s)−ℳ⁡(H,U,Pn​e​g)\mathbf{v}_{diff}=\mathcal{M}(H,U,P_{pos})-\mathcal{M}(H,U,P_{neg}) (1)

This difference vector 𝐯d​i​f​f\mathbf{v}_{diff} is designed to neutralize common-mode noise (e.g., syntax) while isolating the sentiment direction. The geometric properties of 𝐯d​i​f​f\mathbf{v}_{diff} (Norm and Distance) will be further exploited in the subsequent bootstrapping phase.

3.2 Probe-Guided Criteria Bootstrapping

Curating high-quality, behavior-oriented rubrics is traditionally a labor-intensive process requiring expert domain knowledge. To resolve the "cold-start" lack of rubrics, we propose an unsupervised pipeline (Figure 1 Left).

Phase 1: Blind Probing

Lacking specific rubrics, we exploit the model’s inductive bias. We use generic semantic prompts (e.g., "Performance is Excellent/Terrible", see Appendix A) to extract a coarse 𝐯d​i​f​f\mathbf{v}_{diff} using Eq. (1). This vector captures the model’s innate intuition about quality without detailed instructions.

Phase 2: Polarization Mining

To design an effective mining strategy, we first conducted an exploratory analysis on a validation set. As illustrated in Figure 2, we observe two key geometric properties of 𝐯d​i​f​f\mathbf{v}_{diff}:

  1. 1.

    Intensity (Figure 2a): The Euclidean norm ‖𝐯d​i​f​f‖2\|\mathbf{v}_{diff}\|_{2} exhibits a step-wise positive correlation with satisfaction scores.

  2. 2.

    Outlierness (Figure 2b): The Manhattan distance to the centroid follows a U-shaped distribution, where extreme scores are geometrically distant from the center.

Inspired by these findings, we formulate the Polarization Index (PI) to fuse intensity and outlierness:

P​I​(x)=𝒵⁡(‖𝐯d​i​f​f​(x)‖2)×𝒵⁡(‖𝐯d​i​f​f​(x)−𝐜‖1)PI(x)=\mathcal{Z}(\|\mathbf{v}_{diff}(x)\|_{2})\times\mathcal{Z}(\|\mathbf{v}_{diff}(x)-\mathbf{c}\|_{1}) (2)

where we use Manhattan distance for robustness. As shown in Figure 2c, PI effectively pushes extreme scores to the tails. By sampling from the top-KK and bottom-KK PI regions, we boost the mining efficiency of informative cases by an order of magnitude.

Phase 3: Inverse Generation & Deployment

We feed the mined extreme samples into a teacher model (e.g., Qwen3-Max) to reverse-engineer detailed behavior-oriented rubrics. To ensure robustness, we employ an Ensemble Distillation strategy (see Appendix A for the ensemble distillation meta-prompts). This bootstrapped rubric serves as the Standardization Infrastructure: it aligns the teacher model (for pseudo-labeling) and human experts (for verification), ensuring high Inter-Annotator Agreement. Additionally, it provides a "warm-start" baseline for operations teams to fine-tune specific logic (e.g., penalizing "error loops"). Note that bootstrapping is a one-off initialization, incurring zero inference cost.

3.3 Geometry-Aware Regression Probing

With the bootstrapped rubrics, we proceed to curate the training data and train the scorer.

Human-in-the-Loop Annotation

Instead of costly full-manual annotation, we adopt a Human-in-the-Loop strategy. We first use the Teacher LLM (prompted with the bootstrapped rubrics) to generate pseudo-labels for a small subset of data. Human experts then verify and correct these labels. This process ensures high data quality (IAA > 0.90) with minimal effort, providing a reliable supervision signal for the probe.

Refined Extraction

Using these verified samples, we replace the generic blind prompts with the specific, behavior-oriented rubrics generated in Section 3.2 (see Appendix A for the final probing prompt). This extracts a Refined 𝐯d​i​f​f\mathbf{v}_{diff} that captures fine-grained nuances (e.g., distinguishing "polite refusal" from "impolite rejection").

Geometric Resampling

Industrial datasets are heavily skewed towards median scores. Training on such data leads to mode collapse. We propose a Geometric Resampling strategy: down-sampling high-density regions (low distance DcD_{c}) and up-sampling low-density tails. Experiments in Sec 5.1 confirm that this step is crucial for preventing performance collapse.

PLS Regression & Feature Augmentation

We employ PLS regression to map the high-dimensional vector to a continuous score. Unlike PCA (unsupervised), PLS seeks latent directions that maximize covariance with the target score, effectively filtering out topic noise. To further boost performance in small-sample regimes, we exploit the geometric insights from Figure 2a: the Norm (‖𝐯d​i​f​f‖\|\mathbf{v}_{diff}\|) and Distance (Dc​e​n​t​r​o​i​dD_{centroid}) are explicitly concatenated with the latent vector. The augmented input 𝐯~=[𝐯d​i​f​f;‖𝐯d​i​f​f‖;Dc​e​n​t​r​o​i​d]\tilde{\mathbf{v}}=[\mathbf{v}_{diff};\|\mathbf{v}_{diff}\|;D_{centroid}] allows the linear PLS model to efficiently capture the non-linear intensity signals observed in the exploratory analysis.

Uncertainty via Layer-wise Consistency

Beyond point estimation, industrial deployment requires reliability scores. We exploit the model’s internal dynamics by training two separate PLS heads: one on the intermediate layer (e.g., Layer 15, representing intuition) and one on the final layer (e.g., Layer 40, representing reasoning). We define the Uncertainty Score 𝒰\mathcal{U} as the absolute deviation between these layers:

𝒰⁡(x)=|Sf​i​n​a​l​(x)−Sm​i​d​(x)|\mathcal{U}(x)=|S_{final}(x)-S_{mid}(x)| (3)

A high 𝒰\mathcal{U} indicates internal cognitive conflict, serving as an unsupervised proxy for prediction error (analyzed in Sec 5.2).

3.4 High-Throughput Inference Engine

We optimize the inference architecture (Figure 1 Right) to maximize throughput.

Suffix-Only Probing via RadixAttention

Standard evaluation requires re-processing the dialogue history for each rubric. We leverage SGLang’s RadixAttention Zheng et al. (2023), which automatically manages a prefix tree of KV caches. The system computes the shared Prefix (History) once. When evaluating NN different rubrics, SGLang automatically hits the cached prefix node and only computes the task-specific Suffixes. This reduces complexity from O⁡(N⋅Lt​o​t​a​l)O(N\cdot L_{total}) to O⁡(Lp​r​e​f​i​x+N⋅Ls​u​f​f​i​x)O(L_{prefix}+N\cdot L_{suffix}).

Context Compression

For ultra-long contexts, we further apply "Middle-Out" Compression, truncating the redundant middle parts of history. Experiments indicate this reduces prefill costs by ∼64%\sim 64\% without compromising accuracy due to the Recency Bias of LLMs.

Hybrid Deployment Strategy

To maximize ROI, we tailor the deployment precision based on the model size and hardware constraints:

  • •

    Larger Models (>10B): These are typically memory-bound due to KV-cache consumption. We apply INT4-AWQ quantization to minimize weight footprint, allowing for significantly larger batch sizes (concurrency) within the same GPU memory budget.

  • •

    Smaller Models (<10B): These are often compute-bound during the prefill phase. Since the weights fit comfortably in memory, we deploy them in BF16 precision to avoid the computational overhead of dequantization kernels, which our benchmarks show can degrade throughput for smaller architectures.

Ultimately, this architecture achieves an industrial-scale throughput of approx. 1.4M sessions/day (using 8B), reducing costs by >169×>169\times

4 Experiments

We validate BoRP across three dimensions: Accuracy (RQ1), Generalization (RQ2), and Efficiency (RQ3).

4.1 Experimental Setup

Datasets

We utilize two datasets: (1) Expert Industrial Dataset (Internal): Comprises 700 sessions from production logs, manually annotated for User Acceptance by senior experts with high agreement (K-alpha > 0.90). We use this for RQ1 (Main Results).The detailed scoring rubric is provided in Appendix D. (2) HelpSteer2 (Public): To test generalization (RQ2), we focus on the Verbosity dimension of HelpSteer2 Wang et al. (2023b), a challenging metric for generative models.

Baselines

We compare BoRP against two generative paradigms: Gen (Qwen3-14B) and the proprietary SOTA Gen (Qwen3-Max). For fair comparison, we empirically selected the optimal prompt strategy for each model (detailed prompts and sensitivity analysis are in Appendix B).

Implementation

BoRP is built on Qwen3-14B/8B-Chat. The PLS regressor is configured with n=5n=5 components. All experiments run on a single NVIDIA A100 (80GB) (see Appendix E for code snippets and hyperparameter settings).

4.2 Main Results (RQ1)

Table 1 presents the performance on the Industrial Dataset. BoRP (14B) achieves a dominant K-alpha of 0.796 and Pearson correlation of 0.806, significantly outperforming the much larger Gen (Qwen3-Max) (0.733). Notably, even the lightweight BoRP (8B) matches SOTA performance (K-alpha = 0.727). The detailed scoring rubric for "User Acceptance" is provided in Appendix D.

This result strongly supports our hypothesis: by directly probing latent hidden states, BoRP bypasses the "Alignment Tax" (central tendency bias) inherent in generative outputs, thereby unlocking the model’s intrinsic discriminative power. Statistical significance tests (paired t-test) confirm that BoRP’s improvement over Qwen3-Max is statistically significant (p<0.01p<0.01).

4.3 Generalization Analysis (RQ2)

To demonstrate universality, we replicated the BoRP pipeline on HelpSteer2 (Verbosity). We re-trained the PLS head on the training split without modifying the feature extraction architecture.

Results

As shown in Table 2, BoRP (14B) maintains high consistency (K-alpha = 0.695), whereas generative baselines collapse (K-alpha < 0.33) due to severe calibration failures (Score Inflation). This highlights BoRP’s robustness to domain shifts.

Analysis of Generative Failures

An intriguing phenomenon is observed in the generative baselines: Gen (Qwen3-Max) scores a lower K-alpha (0.153) than the weaker Gen (14B) (0.326), yet its Pearson correlation is significantly higher (0.622 vs. 0.451). This discrepancy highlights two distinct failure modes of generative evaluation:

  • •

    Calibration Failure (Qwen3-Max): Despite capturing the correct ranking trend (high Pearson), Qwen3-Max exhibits severe "Score Inflation", systematically over-rating mediocre responses (3-4) as perfect (5). This distributional shift destroys the K-alpha score.

  • •

    Central Tendency Bias (Qwen3-14B): The smaller model adopts a conservative strategy, clustering predictions around the median to minimize risk. While this artificially boosts K-alpha slightly, it lacks true discriminative power.

4.4 Efficiency Analysis (RQ3)

We benchmarked the inference performance on a single A100 (80GB). Baselines Selection: We compare the "standard production configuration" for each paradigm. For generative evaluation, we default to Gen (14B), as smaller models (e.g., 8B) lack the instruction-following capability for complex rubrics. In contrast, since our RQ1 results show that BoRP (8B) matches SOTA performance (K-alpha ≈\approx 0.73), we select the 8B version to highlight BoRP’s unique advantage in enabling model downsizing.

  • •

    Throughput: By synergizing Suffix-Only probing with Context Compression, BoRP (8B) achieves a throughput of 57,800 sessions/hour. This represents a 7.9×\times speedup over the Gen (14B) baseline (7,300 sessions/hour).

  • •

    Cost: Evaluating 100k sessions costs merely $4 (assuming spot pricing), a reduction of >169×>169\times compared to GPT-4o API (see Table 3).

5 Analysis

In this section, we dissect the contribution of each component within BoRP and analyze its internal mechanisms.

5.1 Ablation Studies

We dissect BoRP’s components on the Industrial Dataset (for training strategy) and HelpSteer2 (for rubrics).

Impact of Training Strategy

As shown in Table 4 (Top), Geometric Resampling is critical. Training on the natural long-tail distribution causes performance to collapse (K-alpha = 0.796 →\rightarrow 0.615), confirming that standard supervision fails in extreme imbalance. Furthermore, replacing PLS with unsupervised PCA degrades performance to 0.552, highlighting the necessity of supervised dimensionality reduction.

Efficacy of Bootstrapped Rubrics

Table 4 (Bottom) validates our unsupervised rubric generation. For BoRP, the bootstrapped rubric achieves comparable performance to the expert-curated one (0.674≈0.6950.674\approx 0.695), proving its utility for cold-start. Interestingly, for Gen (Qwen3-Max), AI-generated rubrics even outperform human ones (0.220>0.1530.220>0.153), suggesting better alignment with the model’s intrinsic understanding. For a qualitative comparison between the official and bootstrapped rubrics, refer to Appendix C. Note that bootstrapping samples were strictly excluded from the test set to avoid leakage.

5.2 Uncertainty Quantification

Using the large-scale HelpSteer2 dataset, we analyze the relationship between layer-wise consistency and prediction error. Figure 3 plots the RMSE against the score difference between Layer 40 and Layer 15 (Δ​S\Delta S). We observe a strong positive correlation: samples with low inconsistency (Δ​S≈0\Delta S\approx 0) achieve minimal error (RMSE ≈\approx 0.65), while high-conflict samples (Δ​S>1.5\Delta S>1.5) show high error. This validates Δ​S\Delta S as an effective proxy for model uncertainty.

5.3 Boosting A/B Testing

We integrated BoRP scores as covariates in CUPED to reduce A/B testing variance. Based on 2,300 active users, we observed a correlation of ρ=0.212\rho=0.212 between experiment and historical scores. While moderate, this yields a statistically significant variance reduction of 4.5%. Specifically, for detecting a 0.2% lift, the required sample size drops by approx. 10,000 users (from 235k to 225k). This represents a "free efficiency gain" that scales linearly with traffic, establishing BoRP as a sensitivity multiplier.

6 Conclusion

We introduced BoRP, a geometry-aware framework that breaks the "impossible triangle" of LLM evaluation. By reframing evaluation as a regression task via PLS and automating rubric generation through polarization mining, BoRP achieves expert-level fidelity (K-alpha ≈\approx 0.8) without human intervention. Furthermore, our Suffix-Only inference engine delivers an industrial-scale throughput of approx. 1.4M sessions/day, enabling cost-effective full-traffic monitoring and sensitive A/B testing via CUPED. While highly effective, BoRP’s linear nature may limit its reasoning depth for complex tasks. Future work will explore multi-layer probe fusion and multi-modal extensions to address these challenges.

Abstract
Accurate evaluation of user satisfaction is critical for iterative development of conversational AI. However, for open-ended assistants, traditional A/B testing lacks reliable metrics: explicit feedback is sparse, while implicit metrics are ambiguous.
To bridge this gap, we introduce BoRP ( Bo otstrapped R egression P robing), a scalable framework for high-fidelity satisfaction evaluation. Unlike generative approaches, BoRP leverages the geometric properties of LLM latent space. It employs a polarization-index-based bootstrapping mechanism to automate rubric generation and utilizes Partial Least Squares (PLS) to map hidden states to continuous scores.
Experiments on industrial datasets show that BoRP (Qwen3-8B/14B) significantly outperforms generative baselines (even Qwen3-Max) in alignment with human judgments. Furthermore, BoRP reduces inference costs by orders of magnitude, enabling full-scale monitoring and highly sensitive A/B testing via CUPED.
Figure 1: The BoRP Framework. (Left) Probe-Guided Bootstrapping: Illustration of the Polarization Mining process, extracting extreme samples for rubric generation. (Right) Geometry-Aware Probing Engine: BoRP extracts hidden states via contrastive suffix prompting. A PLS regressor projects the difference vector to a continuous score. Notably, we aggregate signals from both intermediate and final layers to quantify model uncertainty via the layer-wise score gap(see Sec 5 ). This architecture leverages KV-cache reuse, achieving high-throughput evaluation.
1 Introduction
With the advent of LLMs, conversational agents have shifted towards unstructured, open-ended interactions, enabling users to fulfill diverse intents. This flexibility, however, complicates satisfaction quantification. Traditional heuristic metrics (e.g., Session Duration, Turn Counts) suffer from ambiguity Deriu et al. (2021) : prolonged engagement can signal either immersion or confusion. Conversely, posterior metrics like Retention (R1/R7) act as lagging indicators, lacking the sensitivity required for rapid strategy iteration. This creates a critical "Metric Gap": the industry urgently needs a framework to capture immediate satisfaction with high fidelity.
The Dilemma of Existing Paradigms
Existing evaluation methodologies primarily fall into four categories, yet each hits a "hard wall" in industrial deployment.
Manual Evaluation , while serving as the gold standard, is blocked by the Wall of Scalability. The sparsity of human labels results in insufficient statistical power for A/B testing Kohavi et al. (2020) . Consequently, detecting small but meaningful strategy improvements requires impractically long experiment durations.
Generative Evaluation (LLM-as-a-Judge) suffers from an irreconcilable Accuracy-Cost Trade-off. Using SOTA models (e.g., GPT-4) incurs prohibitive costs for full-scale monitoring. Conversely, smaller models (e.g., 7B-14B) often exhibit an "Alignment Tax"—a central tendency bias that suppresses extreme judgments. Furthermore, recent research Zhu et al. (2025) reveals the intrinsic instability of generative judgments, where stochastic decoding leads to inconsistent scores, necessitating expensive aggregation strategies to ensure reliability.
Fine-tuned Evaluators (Specialized Judges & BERT) attempt to bridge the gap by training on evaluation-specific datasets. Recent works like Prometheus Kim et al. (2024) , JudgeLM Zhu et al. (2023) , and JudgeLRM Yuan and others (2025) have shown promise by fine-tuning LLMs on massive feedback datasets (often > 100 ​ k >100k samples) . However, this paradigm faces two hurdles: (1) Data Scalability: Curating such large-scale, high-quality reasoning traces is prohibitively expensive for every new business domain. (2) Inference Cost: Being generative in nature, they still incur high decoding latency. On the other end, traditional discriminative fine-tuning (e.g., BERT) is fast but limited by a Cognitive Bottleneck, lacking the reasoning depth to evaluate complex multi-turn logic in open-ended chat.
Conventional Probing (typically linear classifiers or PCA), while efficient, often settles for Coarse Classification. Even recent works Maiya et al. (2025) focusing on preference extraction remain limited to pairwise ranking or binary judgments. Unsupervised probes are easily distracted by "Topic Residuals"—where the high variance of conversation topics overshadows subtle sentiment signals Burns et al. (2022) , making them unsuitable for fine-grained ordinal regression in industrial settings.
Present Work
To bridge these gaps, we introduce BoRP ( Bo otstrapped R egression P robing), an end-to-end framework designed to break the "impossible triangle" of quality, cost, and coverage in industrial evaluation. We reframe evaluation not as generation, but as a high-fidelity regression task within the latent space.
Contributions
Our main contributions are four-fold:
•
Methodological Innovation: We propose a Geometry-Aware Regression approach. By introducing Partial Least Squares (PLS) Wold (1966) and a Polarization-guided resampling strategy, we effectively identify satisfaction-related subspaces within high-dimensional noise, outperforming PCA and generative baselines in fine-grained scoring.
•
Data Efficiency: We design a Probe-Guided Bootstrapping mechanism. By defining a Polarization Index to unsupervisedly mine extreme samples and employing ensemble distillation, we automate rubric generation, significantly reducing the reliance on expert knowledge.
•
System Performance: We implement a high-throughput inference engine leveraging Suffix-Only Probing and KV-Cache Reuse. This achieves an industrial-scale throughput of approx. 1.4M sessions/day on a single GPU, reducing costs by two orders of magnitude compared to GPT-4.
•
Industrial Impact: We validate BoRP in large-scale online A/B testing. Combined with CUPED , our framework demonstrates superior sensitivity, effectively guiding rapid product iteration.
2 Related Work
LLM-as-a-Judge & Specialized Models
Evaluating open-ended generation has shifted from n-gram metrics (BLEU) to model-based evaluation. Early works prompted proprietary models like GPT-4 Zheng et al. (2024) ; Chang et al. (2024) . Recent efforts focus on fine-tuning specialized judge models, such as Prometheus Kim et al. (2024) , JudgeLM Zhu et al. (2023) , and JudgeLRM Yuan and others (2025) , to improve alignment. While effective, these generative approaches suffer from high inference latency and inherent biases (e.g., position bias Wang et al. (2023a) , verbosity bias Saito et al. (2023) ). Furthermore, recent studies highlight the calibration issues and instability of generative scoring Verga et al. (2025) ; Zhu et al. (2025) . BoRP addresses these by bypassing generation entirely.
Automated Rubric Generation
Defining high-quality rubrics is a bottleneck for evaluation. Recent works like OpenRubrics Zhang et al. (2025) , Auto-Rubric Wang et al. (2025) , and Rubrics-as-Rewards Lee et al. (2025) explore using LLMs to synthesize or refine evaluation criteria. While promising, these methods typically rely on prompting strategies (e.g., "Write a rubric for X"). In contrast, BoRP introduces a Geometry-Guided approach: we use the Polarization Index to mine real-world extreme samples from unlabeled data, ensuring that the generated rubrics are grounded in the actual distribution of the industrial traffic.
Latent Probing & Uncertainty
Probing classifiers have been used to interpret internal representations Alain and Bengio (2016) , detecting truthfulness Burns et al. (2022) or hallucinations. However, most probes focus on binary classification. BoRP advances this by introducing PLS regression for fine-grained ordinal scoring (1-5 scale). Additionally, leveraging insights from uncertainty estimation surveys Huang et al. (2025) ; Chen et al. (2025) , we explore layer-wise consistency as a computation-free proxy for model confidence, enabling reliable human-in-the-loop deployment.
Efficient Inference
Techniques like FlashAttention Dao et al. (2022) and RadixAttention (SGLang) Zheng et al. (2023) have revolutionized throughput. Our work explicitly leverages the KV-Cache separation property of these frameworks to implement our "Suffix-Only" architecture, maximizing the ROI of inference infrastructure.
3 Methodology
We propose BoRP , a geometry-aware framework for scalable LLM evaluation. As illustrated in Figure 1 , the system architecture comprises a Bootstrapping Engine (Figure 1 Left) and a Probing Engine (Figure 1 Right). We detail the mathematical formulation of latent representations in Sec 3.1 , followed by the bootstrapping mechanism (Sec 3.2 ), regression algorithm (Sec 3.3 ), and system optimization (Sec 3.4 ).
3.1 Preliminaries: Contrastive Representation
Following Burns et al. (2022) , we extract representations from the model’s internal states. For a dialogue H H and query U U , we construct a positive prompt P p ​ o ​ s P_{pos} and a negative prompt P n ​ e ​ g P_{neg} (using generic templates initially). We extract the hidden states of the final token at the last layer:
𝐯 d ​ i ​ f ​ f = ℳ ⁡ ( H , U , P p ​ o ​ s ) − ℳ ⁡ ( H , U , P n ​ e ​ g ) \mathbf{v}_{diff}=\mathcal{M}(H,U,P_{pos})-\mathcal{M}(H,U,P_{neg})
(1)
This difference vector 𝐯 d ​ i ​ f ​ f \mathbf{v}_{diff} is designed to neutralize common-mode noise (e.g., syntax) while isolating the sentiment direction. The geometric properties of 𝐯 d ​ i ​ f ​ f \mathbf{v}_{diff} (Norm and Distance) will be further exploited in the subsequent bootstrapping phase.

3.2 Probe-Guided Criteria Bootstrapping
Curating high-quality, behavior-oriented rubrics is traditionally a labor-intensive process requiring expert domain knowledge. To resolve the "cold-start" lack of rubrics, we propose an unsupervised pipeline (Figure 1 Left).
Phase 1: Blind Probing
Lacking specific rubrics, we exploit the model’s inductive bias. We use generic semantic prompts (e.g., "Performance is Excellent/Terrible ", see Appendix A )
to extract a coarse 𝐯 d ​ i ​ f ​ f \mathbf{v}_{diff} using Eq. (1). This vector captures the model’s innate intuition about quality without detailed instructions.
Phase 2: Polarization Mining
To design an effective mining strategy, we first conducted an exploratory analysis on a validation set. As illustrated in Figure 2 , we observe two key geometric properties of 𝐯 d ​ i ​ f ​ f \mathbf{v}_{diff} :
1.
Intensity (Figure 2 a): The Euclidean norm ‖ 𝐯 d ​ i ​ f ​ f ‖ 2 \|\mathbf{v}_{diff}\|_{2} exhibits a step-wise positive correlation with satisfaction scores.
2.
Outlierness (Figure 2 b): The Manhattan distance to the centroid follows a U-shaped distribution, where extreme scores are geometrically distant from the center.
Inspired by these findings, we formulate the Polarization Index (PI) to fuse intensity and outlierness:
P ​ I ​ ( x ) = 𝒵 ⁡ ( ‖ 𝐯 d ​ i ​ f ​ f ​ ( x ) ‖ 2 ) × 𝒵 ⁡ ( ‖ 𝐯 d ​ i ​ f ​ f ​ ( x ) − 𝐜 ‖ 1 ) PI(x)=\mathcal{Z}(\|\mathbf{v}_{diff}(x)\|_{2})\times\mathcal{Z}(\|\mathbf{v}_{diff}(x)-\mathbf{c}\|_{1})
(2)
where we use Manhattan distance for robustness. As shown in Figure 2 c, PI effectively pushes extreme scores to the tails. By sampling from the top- K K and bottom- K K PI regions, we boost the mining efficiency of informative cases by an order of magnitude.
Phase 3: Inverse Generation & Deployment
We feed the mined extreme samples into a teacher model (e.g., Qwen3-Max) to reverse-engineer detailed behavior-oriented rubrics. To ensure robustness, we employ an Ensemble Distillation strategy (see Appendix A for the ensemble distillation meta-prompts).
This bootstrapped rubric serves as the Standardization Infrastructure: it aligns the teacher model (for pseudo-labeling) and human experts (for verification), ensuring high Inter-Annotator Agreement. Additionally, it provides a "warm-start" baseline for operations teams to fine-tune specific logic (e.g., penalizing "error loops"). Note that bootstrapping is a one-off initialization, incurring zero inference cost.
3.3 Geometry-Aware Regression Probing
With the bootstrapped rubrics, we proceed to curate the training data and train the scorer.
Human-in-the-Loop Annotation
Instead of costly full-manual annotation, we adopt a Human-in-the-Loop strategy. We first use the Teacher LLM (prompted with the bootstrapped rubrics) to generate pseudo-labels for a small subset of data. Human experts then verify and correct these labels. This process ensures high data quality (IAA > 0.90) with minimal effort, providing a reliable supervision signal for the probe.
Refined Extraction
Using these verified samples, we replace the generic blind prompts with the specific, behavior-oriented rubrics generated in Section 3.2 (see Appendix A for the final probing prompt). This extracts a Refined 𝐯 d ​ i ​ f ​ f \mathbf{v}_{diff} that captures fine-grained nuances (e.g., distinguishing "polite refusal" from "impolite rejection").
Geometric Resampling
Industrial datasets are heavily skewed towards median scores. Training on such data leads to mode collapse. We propose a Geometric Resampling strategy: down-sampling high-density regions (low distance D c D_{c} ) and up-sampling low-density tails. Experiments in Sec 5.1 confirm that this step is crucial for preventing performance collapse.
PLS Regression & Feature Augmentation
We employ PLS regression to map the high-dimensional vector to a continuous score. Unlike PCA (unsupervised), PLS seeks latent directions that maximize covariance with the target score, effectively filtering out topic noise.
To further boost performance in small-sample regimes, we exploit the geometric insights from Figure 2 a: the Norm ( ‖ 𝐯 d ​ i ​ f ​ f ‖ \|\mathbf{v}_{diff}\| ) and Distance ( D c ​ e ​ n ​ t ​ r ​ o ​ i ​ d D_{centroid} ) are explicitly concatenated with the latent vector. The augmented input 𝐯 ~ = [ 𝐯 d ​ i ​ f ​ f ; ‖ 𝐯 d ​ i ​ f ​ f ‖ ; D c ​ e ​ n ​ t ​ r ​ o ​ i ​ d ] \tilde{\mathbf{v}}=[\mathbf{v}_{diff};\|\mathbf{v}_{diff}\|;D_{centroid}] allows the linear PLS model to efficiently capture the non-linear intensity signals observed in the exploratory analysis.
Uncertainty via Layer-wise Consistency
Beyond point estimation, industrial deployment requires reliability scores. We exploit the model’s internal dynamics by training two separate PLS heads: one on the intermediate layer (e.g., Layer 15, representing intuition ) and one on the final layer (e.g., Layer 40, representing reasoning ). We define the Uncertainty Score 𝒰 \mathcal{U} as the absolute deviation between these layers:
𝒰 ⁡ ( x ) = | S f ​ i ​ n ​ a ​ l ​ ( x ) − S m ​ i ​ d ​ ( x ) | \mathcal{U}(x)=|S_{final}(x)-S_{mid}(x)|
(3)
A high 𝒰 \mathcal{U} indicates internal cognitive conflict, serving as an unsupervised proxy for prediction error (analyzed in Sec 5.2 ).
3.4 High-Throughput Inference Engine
We optimize the inference architecture (Figure 1 Right) to maximize throughput.
Suffix-Only Probing via RadixAttention
Standard evaluation requires re-processing the dialogue history for each rubric. We leverage SGLang’s RadixAttention Zheng et al. (2023) , which automatically manages a prefix tree of KV caches.
The system computes the shared Prefix (History) once. When evaluating N N different rubrics, SGLang automatically hits the cached prefix node and only computes the task-specific Suffixes. This reduces complexity from O ⁡ ( N ⋅ L t ​ o ​ t ​ a ​ l ) O(N\cdot L_{total}) to O ⁡ ( L p ​ r ​ e ​ f ​ i ​ x + N ⋅ L s ​ u ​ f ​ f ​ i ​ x ) O(L_{prefix}+N\cdot L_{suffix}) .
Context Compression
For ultra-long contexts, we further apply "Middle-Out" Compression, truncating the redundant middle parts of history. Experiments indicate this reduces prefill costs by ∼ 64 % \sim 64\% without compromising accuracy due to the Recency Bias of LLMs.
Hybrid Deployment Strategy
To maximize ROI, we tailor the deployment precision based on the model size and hardware constraints:
•
Larger Models (>10B): These are typically memory-bound due to KV-cache consumption. We apply INT4-AWQ quantization to minimize weight footprint, allowing for significantly larger batch sizes (concurrency) within the same GPU memory budget.
•
Smaller Models (<10B): These are often compute-bound during the prefill phase. Since the weights fit comfortably in memory, we deploy them in BF16 precision to avoid the computational overhead of dequantization kernels, which our benchmarks show can degrade throughput for smaller architectures.
Ultimately, this architecture achieves an industrial-scale throughput of approx. 1.4M sessions/day (using 8B), reducing costs by > 169 × >169\times
4 Experiments
We validate BoRP across three dimensions: Accuracy (RQ1), Generalization (RQ2), and Efficiency (RQ3).
4.1 Experimental Setup
Datasets
We utilize two datasets:
(1) Expert Industrial Dataset (Internal): Comprises 700 sessions from production logs, manually annotated for User Acceptance by senior experts with high agreement (K-alpha > 0.90). We use this for RQ1 (Main Results).The detailed scoring rubric is provided in Appendix D .
(2) HelpSteer2 (Public): To test generalization (RQ2), we focus on the Verbosity dimension of HelpSteer2 Wang et al. (2023b) , a challenging metric for generative models.
Baselines
We compare BoRP against two generative paradigms: Gen (Qwen3-14B) and the proprietary SOTA Gen (Qwen3-Max). For fair comparison, we empirically selected the optimal prompt strategy for each model (detailed prompts and sensitivity analysis are in Appendix B ).
Implementation
BoRP is built on Qwen3-14B/8B-Chat. The PLS regressor is configured with n = 5 n=5 components. All experiments run on a single NVIDIA A100 (80GB) (see Appendix E for code snippets and hyperparameter settings).

Results
As shown in Table 2 , BoRP (14B) maintains high consistency (K-alpha = 0.695), whereas generative baselines collapse (K-alpha < 0.33) due to severe calibration failures (Score Inflation). This highlights BoRP’s robustness to domain shifts.
Analysis of Generative Failures
An intriguing phenomenon is observed in the generative baselines: Gen (Qwen3-Max) scores a lower K-alpha (0.153) than the weaker Gen (14B) (0.326), yet its Pearson correlation is significantly higher (0.622 vs. 0.451).
This discrepancy highlights two distinct failure modes of generative evaluation:
•
Calibration Failure (Qwen3-Max): Despite capturing the correct ranking trend (high Pearson), Qwen3-Max exhibits severe "Score Inflation" , systematically over-rating mediocre responses (3-4) as perfect (5). This distributional shift destroys the K-alpha score.
•
Central Tendency Bias (Qwen3-14B): The smaller model adopts a conservative strategy, clustering predictions around the median to minimize risk. While this artificially boosts K-alpha slightly, it lacks true discriminative power.

5.3 Boosting A/B Testing
We integrated BoRP scores as covariates in CUPED to reduce A/B testing variance. Based on 2,300 active users, we observed a correlation of ρ = 0.212 \rho=0.212 between experiment and historical scores. While moderate, this yields a statistically significant variance reduction of 4.5%. Specifically, for detecting a 0.2% lift, the required sample size drops by approx. 10,000 users (from 235k to 225k). This represents a "free efficiency gain" that scales linearly with traffic, establishing BoRP as a sensitivity multiplier.
6 Conclusion
We introduced BoRP, a geometry-aware framework that breaks the "impossible triangle" of LLM evaluation. By reframing evaluation as a regression task via PLS and automating rubric generation through polarization mining, BoRP achieves expert-level fidelity (K-alpha ≈ \approx 0.8) without human intervention. Furthermore, our Suffix-Only inference engine delivers an industrial-scale throughput of approx. 1.4M sessions/day, enabling cost-effective full-traffic monitoring and sensitive A/B testing via CUPED.
While highly effective, BoRP’s linear nature may limit its reasoning depth for complex tasks. Future work will explore multi-layer probe fusion and multi-modal extensions to address these challenges.
